title: Bench Skills
blurb: Hands-on procedures at the lab bench.

topics.name: Measuring Voltage
topics.question: How do I measure voltage across a node with a multimeter
topics.assetAlt: Schematic of a voltage measurement: a voltmeter connected in parallel across resistor R1 in a powered DC circuit that also drives an LED.
topics.summary: Reading a powered node against ground.

sections.heading: Set up the meter
paragraphs: Select DC volts, plug the black lead into COM and the red lead into the V/Ω jack. Voltage is measured *in parallel* — across a component or between a node and ground, with the circuit powered.

sections.heading: Take the reading
paragraphs: Put the black probe on the common ground and the red probe on the node of interest. Start on a range above your expected value (or use autorange) and read once the value settles.

topics.hint: A wildly wrong or negative voltage usually means the probes are on the wrong nodes or your ground reference is floating — re-confirm the black probe is on the same ground as the circuit.

topics.name: Measuring Resistance
topics.question: How do I measure resistance safely without damaging the meter
topics.assetAlt: Right and wrong ways to measure resistance: an ohmmeter across a resistor still wired into a powered circuit is crossed out; measuring the resistor after isolating it from the circuit is marked correct.
topics.summary: Reading resistance in Ω on an unpowered part.

sections.heading: Power off first
paragraphs: Resistance is measured on an *unpowered* circuit or an isolated component. Measuring a live circuit gives meaningless readings and can damage the meter. Set the dial to Ω.

sections.heading: Isolate the component
paragraphs: For an accurate value, lift one leg of the component out of the circuit so parallel paths don't skew the reading. Use this to confirm resistor values and identify stepper coil pairs.

topics.hint: A resistance reading lower than the marked value usually means another path is in parallel — lift one leg of the component out of the circuit and measure again.

topics.name: Building a Divider
topics.question: How do I build a sensor voltage divider on a breadboard
topics.assetAlt: Breadboard build of a voltage divider: battery packs feed the power rails, two series resistors meet at a middle node, and jumper wires tap the output, annotated with the measured Vout.
topics.summary: Wiring a sensor + resistor to an analog pin.

sections.heading: The layout
paragraphs: Run 5 V to one end, ground to the other, and place the sensor and fixed resistor in series between them. The junction between the two parts is your output — wire it to an analog pin such as A0.

sections.heading: Sanity check
paragraphs: Before trusting code, measure the junction with a multimeter as you change the sensed quantity. The voltage should move smoothly between roughly 0 V and 5 V.

topics.hint: If the analog pin reads flat, probe the divider junction directly — no movement there means a wiring break or a fixed resistor that swamps the sensor.

topics.name: Wiring a Bridge
topics.question: How do I wire and null a Wheatstone bridge before amplifying
topics.assetAlt: Simulated wiring of a Wheatstone bridge: four resistors on a breadboard powered by a 9 V battery, with a multimeter connected across the two bridge midpoints to read the differential output.
topics.summary: Balancing a bridge to ≈0 V at rest.

sections.heading: Build and excite
paragraphs: Wire the four arms into the diamond, apply a stable excitation voltage across one diagonal, and take the differential output from the other. With the active element at rest the output should sit near zero.

sections.heading: Null the offset
paragraphs: Real resistors never match exactly, so trim one arm (or subtract the offset in software) until the resting output reads ≈0 V. Only then does the amplified signal represent the change you care about.

topics.hint: A bridge whose amplified output saturates immediately was never nulled — bring the resting differential to ≈0 V before the gain stage, not after.

topics.name: Calibrating Sensors
topics.question: How do I calibrate an analog sensor to a real-world value
topics.assetAlt: Calibration curve for a temperature sensor: measured sensor output voltage plotted against temperature, with experimental data points falling close to a straight-line fit.
topics.summary: Mapping raw counts to meaning.

sections.heading: Capture two anchors
paragraphs: Record the raw ADC value at two known conditions — for a moisture probe, fully dry and fully wet; for an LDR, dark and bright. These anchor the range your sensor actually uses.

sections.heading: Map and threshold
paragraphs: Use `map()` between the anchors to convert raw counts to a meaningful scale, and pick any control threshold from real measured readings rather than a guessed number.

topics.hint: A sensor that reads "correct" indoors but fails in the real setting was calibrated against the wrong anchors — re-capture the extremes in the actual environment.

topics.name: Power & Ground
topics.question: How do I set up power rails and a common ground
topics.assetAlt: Isometric breadboard illustration outlining the red and blue power rails that distribute supply and ground along the board — the common reference every measurement and signal in the circuit shares.
topics.summary: A shared reference for every part.

sections.heading: Shared reference
paragraphs: Every measurement and signal is relative to ground. When a sensor, the Arduino, and an external supply all share a single common ground, voltages mean the same thing everywhere.

sections.heading: Separate supplies
paragraphs: Motors and servos should draw from their own supply, but that supply's ground must still be tied to the Arduino ground — otherwise signals and readings drift unpredictably.

topics.hint: Signals that drift once an external supply is added almost always mean the grounds were never tied together — bond every ground to one common rail.

topics.name: Calculated Versus Measured Values
topics.question: Why do measured values differ from calculated ones, and how do you compare them
topics.summary: Why real measurements deviate from ideal calculations and how to quantify the gap.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: Calculated values assume ideal components and controlled conditions. Measured values include tolerance, sensor variation, supply variation, meter accuracy, and contact resistance.

topics.hint: Percent difference = `abs(measured - calculated) / abs(calculated) * 100%`.
